propositions.text: Seeks judicial review of a visa officer’s decision denying her temporary work permit/visa application under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a visa officer’s decision to deny her application for a temporary work permit/visa under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program [the Program] in Canada.

propositions.text: Argues the visa officer’s decision was unreasonable given credible evidence to the contrary.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the visa officer’s decision was unreasonable in light of credible evidence to the contrary.

propositions.text: Disagrees with the Applicant’s position.
propositions.quote: The Respondent disagrees.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a denied work permit, arguing unreasonableness, while the Respondent disagrees.

propositions.text: Parties disagree whether the visa officer should have communicated with the Applicant about concerns with her application.
propositions.quote: The parties also disagree as to whether the visa officer should have communicated with the Applicant to address concerns related to her visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The parties dispute whether the visa officer should have contacted the Applicant about concerns with her application.

propositions.text: Judicial review application is allowed for reasons set out below.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed for the reasons set out below.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application for judicial review, with reasons to follow.

propositions.text: Applicant was born October 22, 1991, is Nigerian, and worked as a childcare attendant in Delta State/Effurun Sapele, Nigeria from March 2015 to December 2018.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was born on October 22, 1991 and is a citizen of Nigeria. From March 2015 to December 2018, the Applicant worked as a childcare attendant at a group of schools in the Delta State/Effurun Sapele region of Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant is a Nigerian citizen born in 1991 who worked as a childcare attendant in Nigeria from 2015 to 2018.

propositions.text: On May 14, 2018, Applicant and a Fort McMurray employer signed a contract for her to work as a live-in caregiver for 24 months.
propositions.quote: On May 14, 2018, the Applicant and her prospective employer, a resident of Fort McMurray, Alberta, entered into a Temporary Foreign Worker Program In-Home Caregiver Employer/Employee Contract [the Contract].

propositions.text: Applicant’s tasks included childcare, light housekeeping, meal preparation, and 44 hours per week of work.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s tasks would include childcare, light housekeeping and meal preparation. The Contract also specified that the Applicant would work 44 hours per week.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant signed a 24-month live-in caregiver contract in Fort McMurray, with duties including childcare and housekeeping, working 44 hours weekly.

propositions.text: On May 16, 2018, the employer applied for an LMIA for the Applicant’s position.
propositions.quote: On May 16, 2018, the prospective employer submitted a Labour Market Impact Assessment [LMIA] application for the position to be occupied by the Applicant.

propositions.text: On June 19, 2018, the Applicant received a positive LMIA, indicating a positive or neutral impact on the Canadian labour market.
propositions.quote: On June 19, 2018, Employment and Social Development Canada/Service Canada sent a letter informing her that she received a positive LMIA.

paragraphs.summary: The employer applied for an LMIA for the Applicant, who received a positive LMIA in June 2018.

propositions.text: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant applied for a temporary work permit/visa, including the LMIA number, and stated no travel in past five years.
propositions.quote: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant requested a temporary work permit/visa under the Program so as to begin her employment under the Contract. The LMIA number was included on the visa application form. In her application for temporary residence, the Applicant indicated that she had not travelled to any country or territory in the past five years.

propositions.text: The visa application did not include information about her assets or available funds.
propositions.quote: The visa application did not contain information pertaining to her assets or available funds.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant applied for a work permit in August 2018, disclosed no recent travel, and did not provide asset or funds information.

propositions.text: On November 30, 2018, a visa officer denied the Applicant’s work permit/visa application.
propositions.quote: In a letter dated November 30, 2018, a visa officer with the Visa Section of the Canadian High Commission in London, United Kingdom, advised the Applicant that her application for a temporary work permit/visa had been denied [the Decision].

propositions.text: Visa officer found the application did not meet IRPA and IRPR requirements for three reasons: travel history, limited employment prospects in Nigeria, and personal assets/financial status.
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on your travel history. - I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on the limited employment prospects in your country of residence. - I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on your personal assets and financial status.

paragraphs.summary: A visa officer denied the Applicant's work permit, citing travel history, employment prospects, and financial status as reasons under IRPR 216(1).

propositions.text: GCMS Notes state Applicant sought caregiver work, showed no proof of funds/assets or travel history, and earned 20,000 naira/month in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: Applicant seeking to work as caregiver, caring for two children under the age of two. Applicant shows no proof of funds/assets, or of previous travel history. Currently working in daycare section of a school, making 20,000 naira (approx. $75 Canadian) per month.

propositions.text: Visa officer was not satisfied Applicant was sufficiently established to motivate return to country of residence, given travel history, funds, and employment opportunities.
propositions.quote: Given Applicant’s travel history, funds, and employment opportunities in COR versus in Canada, I am not satisfied that Applicant is sufficiently established to motivate a return to COR at the end of period authorized for stay.

propositions.text: Application was refused for these reasons.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, application is refused.

paragraphs.summary: GCMS notes show the officer cited lack of funds, travel history, and low salary as reasons for refusing the application.

propositions.text: Did the visa officer act reasonably in denying the Applicant’s work permit/visa application?
propositions.quote: Did the visa officer act reasonably in denying the Applicant’s work permit/visa application?

propositions.text: Did the visa officer breach procedural fairness by not communicating concerns to the Applicant?
propositions.quote: Did the visa officer commit a breach of procedural fairness in not communicating with the Applicant to address concerns related to her visa application?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two issues: reasonableness of the denial and possible breach of procedural fairness by the visa officer.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard applies to the first issue; decision must be within a range of acceptable outcomes and be justified, transparent, and intelligible.
propositions.quote: The first issue engages the reasonableness standard of review, requiring the decision to fall “within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law.”

paragraphs.summary: The court applies the reasonableness standard to the first issue, requiring the decision to be justified and within acceptable outcomes.

propositions.text: Visa officer’s discretionary decisions on work permits are entitled to high deference due to factual nature and officer’s expertise.
propositions.quote: Thus, discretionary decisions of this type are entitled to a high degree of deference since they usually involve questions of fact and relate to a visa officer’s recognized expertise

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that visa officers' discretionary decisions on work permits are given high deference due to their expertise and factual nature.

propositions.text: Visa officers must provide adequate reasons, even if minimal, that justify their decision; reasons must allow the court to understand and review the decision.
propositions.quote: the visa officer must nonetheless provide adequate reasons that justify his or her decision

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers must provide sufficient reasons for their decisions to allow the court to understand and review them.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issue is reviewed on a correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Regarding the procedural fairness issue, the standard of review is correctness

paragraphs.summary: The procedural fairness issue is reviewed on a correctness standard by the court.

propositions.text: Level of procedural fairness owed by visa officers is relaxed due to the nature of the visa application process.
propositions.quote: the level of procedural fairness owed by the visa officer is relaxed, considering the nature of the administrative process for visa applications

paragraphs.summary: The court states that procedural fairness owed by visa officers is relaxed due to the nature of visa applications.

propositions.text: Visa officer failed to give weight to her employment history and recommendation letter, misconstrued her application, and erred regarding travel history.
propositions.quote: She argues that the visa officer failed to give weight to her previous employment history in Nigeria and her letter of recommendation, misconstrued the nature of the Applicant’s work permit application, and erred in drawing a negative inference from the Applicant’s lack of travel history.

propositions.text: Visa officer was not alive to the evidence and failed to provide sufficient reasons for rejecting her application.
propositions.quote: In essence, the Applicant argues that the visa officer was not alive to what was before him and failed to provide sufficient reasons to justify his decision to reject the Applicant’s visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the officer ignored key evidence, misconstrued her application, and failed to provide sufficient reasons for refusal.

propositions.text: Visa officer considered all relevant factors and made a reasonable decision, including considering salary, marital status, and Nigeria’s economic conditions.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the visa officer considered all of the relevant factors and rendered a reasonable decision. The Respondent argues that the visa officer was reasonable when he considered the Applicant’s low salary in Nigeria, her status as a single woman, and the economic conditions in Nigeria when deciding to refuse the Applicant’s work permit application.

propositions.text: Visa officers are not required to provide detailed reasons for their decisions.
propositions.quote: The Respondent further states that visa officers are not required to provide detailed reasons in support of their decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent claims the officer considered all relevant factors and is not required to provide detailed reasons for refusal.

propositions.text: Deficiencies in reasons by administrative decision-makers are closely tied to reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: issues related to “alleged deficiencies or flaws in the reasons” given by an administrative decision-maker are intimately associated with reasonableness review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that flaws in reasons are closely linked to the reasonableness standard of review.

propositions.text: Visa applicants must rebut the presumption they intend to immigrate and must convince the officer they will leave Canada after their stay.
propositions.quote: the burden is upon visa applicants to rebut the presumption that they are immigrants seeking to remain in Canada, and to convince a visa officer that they will leave Canada at the end of their stay

paragraphs.summary: Applicants must rebut the presumption of immigrant intent and convince the officer they will leave Canada after their stay.

propositions.text: There is a presumption that applicants are immigrants; applicants must rebut it.
propositions.quote: there is a legal presumption according to which any person seeking to enter Canada is presumed to be an immigrant; it is up to the applicant to rebut this presumption

propositions.text: The court should not re-weigh the evidence.
propositions.quote: it is not for the Court to re-weigh the evidence

propositions.text: The officer is presumed to have reviewed all evidence unless shown otherwise and need not reference every document submitted.
propositions.quote: the Officer is presumed to have reviewed all of the evidence unless the contrary is shown (Florea v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1993] FCJ No 598 (QL) (FCA)) and is not required to make reference to every document submitted (Hassan v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1992), 147 NR 317, [1992] FCJ No 946 (QL) (FCA); Zhou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 465 at para 20

propositions.text: The officer’s reasons include the form, letter, and GCMS notes.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s reasons for decision include the form and the letter, as well as the GCMS notes prepared for the case.

paragraphs.summary: Precedent establishes applicants are presumed immigrants, courts don't re-weigh evidence, officers are presumed to review all evidence, and reasons include forms and notes.

propositions.text: The visa officer found the Applicant did not show she would leave Canada at the end of her work contract.
propositions.quote: the visa officer found that the Applicant did not meet her burden to show that she would leave Canada at the end of her work contract.

propositions.text: This was based on lack of evidence of funds, absence of travel history, and poor employment prospects in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: This determination was made on the basis of the Applicant’s lack of evidence of funds, absence of travel history, and poor employment prospects in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier visa officer denied the visa because the Applicant lacked evidence of funds, travel history, and had poor employment prospects in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Visa officers commonly use templates for decisions, which is acceptable for efficiency.
propositions.quote: I accept that it has become commonplace for visa officers to use templates in rendering their decisions, especially when faced with a high volume of applications.

propositions.text: Visa officers have wide discretion and may use objective criteria in decisions.
propositions.quote: I also accept that visa officers enjoy a wide berth of discretion in making their decisions and may take into account objective criteria

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts visa officers use templates for efficiency and have wide discretion to use objective criteria in decisions.

propositions.text: Visa officers using templates must modify them to show their reasoning and address contradictory evidence.
propositions.quote: visa officers should bring the necessary modifications or render reasons that would indicate their thought process in an intelligible manner, and address evidence that may contradict important findings of fact.

propositions.text: In this case, the visa officer did not explain how the evidence was interpreted to reach the decision.
propositions.quote: the visa officer did not establish the basis for understanding how he interpreted the evidence to arrive at his decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds visa officers must explain their reasoning, and this officer did not show how evidence was interpreted to reach the decision.

propositions.text: The visa officer's reasons are hurried and do not explain the decision-making process.
propositions.quote: The visa officer’s reasons are rather hurried, and do not explain the thought process that underlies his decision to refuse the work visa.

propositions.text: The officer referenced the wrong IRPR section, likely due to template error, but this is not fatal as GCMS Notes align with work permit criteria.
propositions.quote: Although this may suggest inattention and a hurried approach, in and of itself it is not fatal in this case as the remarks in the GCMS Notes seem to be in line with work permit application criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's reasons hurried and referencing the wrong law, but this error is not fatal since the notes align with work permit criteria.

propositions.text: The decision has several shortcomings.
propositions.quote: the Decision does suffer from a series of shortcomings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the decision has several shortcomings.

propositions.text: The visa officer failed to give sufficient weight to the Applicant's employment history in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: the visa officer failed to give sufficient weight to evidence showing that the Applicant had a reasonable employment history in Nigeria.

propositions.text: The officer did not explain how the Applicant's employment history negatively impacts future prospects, despite positive evidence.
propositions.quote: the visa officer does not mention how this fact negatively impacts future employment prospects, in particular given the Applicant’s positive letter of recommendation from her current employer, nor does he mention the Applicant’s training certificates and over three years of employment in Nigeria.

propositions.text: These factors could displace the finding of poor employment prospects and should have been addressed.
propositions.quote: These are all relevant factors which may well go to displacing a finding that the Applicant had poor employment prospects in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Given the officer's emphasis on limited prospects, he should have addressed the Applicant's employment history.
propositions.quote: it seems to me that the visa officer in this case should have specifically addressed the Applicant’s current employment history.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to address the Applicant's positive employment history, which could counter the finding of poor prospects in Nigeria.

propositions.text: The officer drew a negative inference from the Applicant's salary without context about living standards in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: there is nothing in the GCMS Notes that contextualizes the Applicant’s salary in Nigeria against living standards in that country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer negatively inferred from the Applicant's salary without context about Nigerian living standards.

propositions.text: Better job opportunities in Canada are common for applicants from lower-income countries.
propositions.quote: such is the case for most applicants in similar circumstances coming from countries with a significantly lower standard of living than Canada.

propositions.text: Stating salary and limited prospects without addressing stable employment history makes it hard to justify the officer's conclusion.
propositions.quote: by simply asserting that there are limited employment prospects in Nigeria without addressing the evidence of the Applicant’s stable employment history, makes it very difficult to say that the conclusion of the visa officer is justified, transparent and intelligible

propositions.text: The court cannot determine if the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: does not allow me to determine whether the conclusion reached is within the range of acceptable outcomes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's reasoning unjustified, as it ignores the Applicant's stable employment and does not show the conclusion is acceptable.

propositions.text: The officer cited limited funds but ignored the Applicant's job offer in Canada with salary and benefits.
propositions.quote: the visa officer also cites the Applicant’s limited funds upon arrival as a factor justifying the denial of the Applicant’s visa application, but without any mention of the fact that the Applicant is coming to Canada with a job in hand with the prospect of earning $598.40 per week plus benefits (room and board included).

propositions.text: The court cannot assess the officer's reasoning without comment on how the job offer affects the sufficiency of funds criterion.
propositions.quote: I cannot assess the visa officer’s reasoning without further comment on his part on how the job in hand in Canada would not otherwise render the criterion of the sufficiency of funds as having been met.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer ignored the Applicant's job offer in Canada when assessing funds, making the reasoning unassessable.

propositions.text: Further comment on funds may not be needed for study permits, but is needed for this work permit case.
propositions.quote: I would think it would be in a case such as this one.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds further comment on funds is needed in this work permit case, unlike for study permits.

propositions.text: The officer unreasonably assessed the Applicant's lack of travel history as a reason to deny the application.
propositions.quote: the visa officer did not act reasonably in assessing the Applicant’s travel history as a further reason to deny the application.

propositions.text: Federal Court has held lack of travel history should be neutral for likelihood of returning to home country.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has consistently held that a work permit applicant’s lack of travel history should be treated as a neutral factor in terms of the his or her likelihood of returning to their country of citizenship

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer unreasonably used lack of travel history against the Applicant, contrary to Federal Court precedent.

propositions.text: It is an error for a visa officer to use lack of travel history as a negative factor for return likelihood.
propositions.quote: It is thus an error for a visa officer to use the Applicant’s lack of previous travel history as a negative factor in determining whether the Applicant will not leave Canada after her employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it is an error to use lack of travel history as a negative factor for return likelihood.

propositions.text: It is within the visa officer's discretion to assign weight to evidence.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that it is within the visa officer’s discretion to assign degree of weight to the evidence

propositions.text: The officer should have given reasons to allow the Court to assess if the outcome fits justification, transparency, and intelligibility principles.
propositions.quote: the visa officer should have in this case articulated even short reasons so as to allow this Court to assess whether the overall outcome fits “comfortably within the principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues discretion on evidence weight, but the court finds the officer should have given reasons for justification and transparency.

propositions.text: The officer was not attuned to the nature and content of the Applicant's work permit application.
propositions.quote: I find that the visa officer was not attuned to the nature and content of the Applicant’s work permit application.

propositions.text: The court understands what the officer is saying, but not why, and it is important to know why.
propositions.quote: Although I understand what the visa officer is saying, I do not understand why he is saying it; it is important that I do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer was not attuned to the application and did not explain the reasoning behind the decision.

propositions.text: The officer should have called the Applicant to allow her to respond to concerns before rejecting the application.
propositions.quote: the Applicant argues that the visa officer should have at least made a telephone call to the Applicant so as to allow her to respond to his concerns about her visa application prior to rejecting it.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the officer should have called her to address concerns before rejecting the application.

propositions.text: Visa application processes are less formal and the duty of fairness is relaxed.
propositions.quote: the process is at the lower end of detail and formality, and the duty of fairness regarding the visa application process is relaxed.

propositions.text: The FCA explained several factors for limited duty of fairness in visa applications, including no legal right to a visa and less serious impact.
propositions.quote: several factors account for this limited duty of fairness, namely, “the absence of a legal right to a visa; the imposition on the Applicant of the burden of establishing eligibility for a visa; the less serious impact on the individual that the refusal of a visa typically has, compared with the removal of a benefit.”

propositions.text: The FCA cautioned against imposing procedural formality that would hinder efficient administration due to high application volume.
propositions.quote: The FCA went on to caution against “imposing a level of procedural formality that, given the volume of applications that visa officers are required to process, would unduly encumber efficient administration”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds visa applications have a relaxed duty of fairness, as explained by the FCA, due to several factors and efficiency concerns.

propositions.text: Additional communication may be needed if the officer doubts credibility, relies on extrinsic evidence, or uses broad generalizations.
propositions.quote: Additional communication with a visa applicant may be appropriate in certain circumstances, say where the visa officer harbours doubts as to the credibility of the evidence provided or the sincerity of testimonial evidence, or if the officer relies on extrinsic evidence that is outside the visa officer’s general expertise or relies on overly broad generalizations or stereotypes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds extra communication may be needed if the officer doubts credibility, uses extrinsic evidence, or relies on generalizations.

propositions.text: In Wang, a phone call may have been appropriate to let the applicant respond to concerns about support and bona fides.
propositions.quote: In that case, this Court found that the visa officer should have provided the Applicant with an opportunity to respond to concerns about the “sincerity of [the Applicant’s] cousin’s offer of support, and [the Applicant’s] bona fides as a temporary visitor to Canada”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that in Wang, a phone call was appropriate to let the applicant respond to concerns about support and bona fides.

propositions.text: A visa officer should inform the applicant of concerns when using extrinsic evidence for the decision.
propositions.quote: A visa officer should also inform the Applicant of his or her concerns when he or she obtains extrinsic evidence that may be used to support the final decision

paragraphs.summary: The court finds officers should inform applicants of concerns when using extrinsic evidence for decisions.

propositions.text: Visa officers may not justify decisions on cultural or regional generalizations without letting the applicant respond.
propositions.quote: visa officers may not justify their decisions on cultural or regional generalizations without allowing the applicant to respond

paragraphs.summary: The court finds officers cannot justify decisions on cultural or regional generalizations without letting the applicant respond.

propositions.text: The Court has consistently rejected that an applicant has the right to clarify or respond to the merits of a visa officer’s decision.
propositions.quote: this Court has consistently rejected the argument that an applicant has the right to clarify his or her application or respond to the merits of the visa officer’s decision

propositions.text: Ling v Canada, Li, and Wen v Canada are cited as authority for this rule.
propositions.quote: Ling v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1198 at paragraph 16; Li; Wen v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCT 1262.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants generally cannot clarify or respond to visa officer decisions, citing prior cases as authority.

propositions.text: The present case does not fall within exceptions that require a heightened duty of fairness.
propositions.quote: The factual circumstances of the present case do not fall within one of the exceptions that give rise to a heightened duty of fairness.

propositions.text: There is no evidence the visa officer doubted the applicant’s credibility or relied on generalizations about her or her country.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence to suggest that the visa officer had doubts as to the credibility, veracity, or sincerity of the Applicant’s evidence or that he relied upon broad generalizations about the Applicant’s personal characteristics or country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no heightened duty of fairness applies, as there is no evidence of credibility concerns or improper generalizations by the visa officer.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not err by not giving the applicant a chance to further justify her visa application.
propositions.quote: I find that the visa officer did not err in not providing the Applicant with an opportunity to further justify her visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer was not required to let the applicant further justify her application.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of the decision’s basis, making it impossible to assess if the outcome was reasonable.
propositions.quote: the visa officer did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of the basis for his decision, and the reasons given fail to allow me to determine whether the conclusion reached is within the range of acceptable outcomes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's reasons were unclear and do not allow assessment of the decision's reasonableness.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed; the visa officer’s decision is set aside and remitted to a different officer for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed, the decision of the visa officer is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination.

propositions.text: No certified question was submitted or arose.
propositions.quote: The parties did not submit a certified question and none arose.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review, sets aside the visa officer's decision, remits the matter, and notes no certified question arises.
